quotes.text: Well, when we were doing the six-hour song, that all started out as a very practical idea to have this song that would play, and it would accompany this Strobo animation toy that we were presenting it with. So we went, "We'll make a song that plays for a couple hours so you could play with this thing, have some friends over to your house and you could play with this thing all night," you know? Then a couple hours turned into like, "Well, how many hours would it be?" And I just sort of flippantly said, "Let's just make it six hours," and just thought that that would be a good time to play with the toy if you were taking some drugs or something. You know, just something a little bit more extreme.

And by coincidence, before I even knew this, Steven [Drozd] had a song that he had been playing around with that already went 25 minutes. I remember when I got with him after that, he was like, "Yeah, I've got this thing that goes 25 minutes, but it feels like it's just five. It just jumbles along." So, with that, we easily said, "Well, let's see if we can work on this same theme, the same 25-30 minutes that he had, and then we'd make that into the six-hour song."

But you get into something like a six-hour song, and then it's a motherf****r. You know, everything you do is like, "Jesus!" We're used to doing -- even long songs for us would be 12 or 13 minutes, sometimes 20 minutes or whatever. You get into these things where you're just going for hours and hours. But, like a lot of things that you do, once you get into it you struggle with it, and you have to fight your way through it and discover new things. It kind of changes you, or changes you for a little while.

So while we were kind of drunk on the challenge or the joys or the failures of the six-hour song, we started to think we would do a 24-hour song, not really knowing the limits of any of the technology or anything like that, but just starting to think, you know, this is absurd or it just takes you to another dimension.

I mean, there were times when we even talked about doing a song that would last for a month. It would go for two, three days, maybe a week or a month, but then I think as we started to look more into the technology, even for the six-hour song, some of that was already pushed to the limits with how we could have anybody else ever hear it or what format it could be in. And the 24-hour song just seemed like a cool concept, to think that you're sitting there for an entire day and night and that it would represent this day.

I had been considering a long sort of sound-Odyssey poem about death. It started to look like we could release it on Halloween, and I was able to -- I had been messing around with these actual human skulls, you know, a big collaboration of coincidences that had led us to it.

We had already booked some time up at Dave Fridmann's studio. So, to make the long answer longer, you get a lot of things set up to where once you get in there, the moments of doubt are kind of pushed along by, "Well, we have to do this! We're already doing this. We already have six-hours done. It's going to be that big of a deal," or, "We already have 13 hours done. We might as well push through."
I think it's like a lot of things. You want some inertia lighting the path ahead of you. So if you do run into these sort of uncertain times, you push through it.

I would say we've done a lot of recording. We've been a band since 1983, and we've done like 14 records or something like that. We've been down that dark, "Fuck-I-don't-know-what-I'm-going-to-do" path a million times. Sometimes those are the things that make the most interesting music or the most unique music.

In the end, we would never think that we couldn't do it. We would probably say that something is not the greatest thing in the world, but I think we're not trying to make the greatest thing in the world. Sometimes we want to see where the thing takes us.

So, that would probably be the answer. This idea that we're pushed along from one experiment to the next, that really makes a lot of difference. I think if we'd had done the six-hour song and then contemplated what we're going to do for a couple years after that -- or thought about the 24-hour song but didn't do it immediately -- I don't think some of that perception of how to do it would have stayed.

Well, it starts off that way. But I have consulted with Dave Fridmann, and he's good with all this technical junk. Our computer guy has a couple of other pretty sophisticated helpers helping him out; that would be George, my computer guy. So, between them, I think when I decided that we were going to do the six-hour song, we would easily jump ahead to be like, "Could we do a song that lasts a month?" And they'd be like, "I don't know. Let's see what we can do." So I think we had arrived, even previous to starting it, that we could do it.
But it's mostly that it's just a lot of f*****g music to always keep track of.

I think at Dave's studio there are three ProTools setups. So while we're working in one studio, Michael has other studios set up. I've been in the room where we can be doing overdubs on one thing while doing overdubs on another thing. Some of it, I have to credit to the way my dentist in Oklahoma City works.
